idiom_name: abstract Component + role dictionary keyed by role spec (Type); DispatchProxy for dynamic role views
implementation_notes: C# has no language-level per-instance extension, so the classic structure is hand-written: a Component abstraction with AddRole/GetRole/RemoveRole/HasRole, a CustomerCore that owns a Dictionary<Type, CustomerRole> and creates roles through a factory delegate (so it never references concrete role types), and an abstract CustomerRole that holds the core and forwards its operations. When clients must receive a single object implementing an arbitrary combination of role interfaces, System.Reflection.DispatchProxy.Create<T, TProxy>() generates that view at runtime and routes every call to the proxy's Invoke method; choose it only when interface-only dispatch is enough, because the generated type hides the concrete role class and works with interfaces alone.
pitfalls: Keying the role dictionary by Type allows only one instance per role class; use an explicit role specification (enum or key) when roles are parametrized.
Roles holding the core and the core holding its roles form a cycle: the GC collects it, but finalizers and unmanaged resources stay alive longer than expected.
DispatchProxy-generated views implement interfaces only - role state, non-public members and the concrete role class are unreachable through the view.
